name: David Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, David. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start around ten doing parcel blocks for one of the app companies, usually four hours around Halford and the villages. Then from five I switch the app over and do takeaway till eleven, mostly pizza and curry. The app made me a zone captain last year, which means I help new couriers set up and I get a small bonus for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the regulars, like the old man on Mill Lane who tips in coins and always asks about the football. Bad is the waiting outside restaurants with the app showing zero orders, because waiting isn't paid. And my car is a 2012 hatchback with 190,000 miles, so every rattle is a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, but the fight was never really about robots, it was about how the apps treat us. I'd post something like that in our couriers' chat. Most of the lads would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, which is tight but liveable. My partner Sofia works in a care home, so between us we cover the flat. The only real risk is the car or the app cutting rates again like it did last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing parcels by day and food by night. I'd keep pushing the courier union campaign for paid waiting time, which is the one thing that would make a real difference. And I'd try to put fifty a month into a car fund, because when the gearbox goes, that's a week's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit flat, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the app cut rates last spring. How much did that hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifteen percent on the food side. We went from a base of £3.40 a drop to £2.90, and they called it a pricing update. Nobody voted on it, it just showed up one Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in your house if the car does go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia drives me in before her shift and I do parcels on her car on her days off, which is a mess. We'd probably put the repair on a card. We did that once already and it took most of a year to clear.

say: The fight was always about **how apps treat couriers**, not about robots.
Couriers need **paid waiting time**, whatever happens with AI.
think: Life stays **tight but liveable** because Sofia's care home wage covers half the flat.
The real risks are the **old car** and another app rate cut.
do: Keep **parcels by day** and takeaway at night.
Push the courier union campaign for **paid waiting**.
Save **fifty a month** in a car repair fund.
feel: **Flat but okay**, without fear but without much hope of change.
S0.quote: We went from a base of £3.40 a drop to £2.90, and they called it a pricing update.
fieldNote: A second income from his partner gives him **more breathing room** than many couriers.
He frames everything as **app power**, not technology.
A single **car repair** already went on a card once and took a year to clear.

steps.text: Keep parcel blocks by day and takeaway shifts at night
Campaign with the courier union for paid waiting time
Put fifty pounds a month into a car repair fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the apps will use this to squeeze us even harder. They'll have AI deciding pay per drop every minute, and nobody to complain to when it goes wrong. I'd post that the union needs to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the driving itself stays human for a while, but the bits around it change. My zone captain role is mostly answering new couriers' questions, and a chatbot could do that tomorrow. So I'd lose the bonus first, then later maybe the driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools a bit more myself, like I already ask a chatbot to help with emails to the council. I'd look at the bus driver training the county runs, since buses feel more solid than apps. And I'd go to every union meeting, because if pay gets set by a computer, we need rules on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like the ground is tilting a bit. I don't panic easily, but this one sits with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The bus training: is that real, or just an idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real, the county pays the licence if you sign for two years. Mo, a lad from our chat, did it last year. He says the hours are worse but the pay doesn't change week to week, which sounds like a dream to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sofia's job change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, she's lifting and washing people, and the paperwork going to a computer might even help her. So she'd be the steady one, which she already sort of is. I'd feel bad leaning on her more, though.

say: Apps will use AI to set **pay per drop** minute by minute.
The union must get **rules on algorithms** before they spread.
think: My **zone captain** bonus goes first, because a chatbot can answer new couriers.
The **driving** stays human longer, but the money around it shrinks.
do: Use **AI tools** a bit more for emails and forms.
Apply for the county's **free bus licence** scheme.
Attend every **union meeting** about algorithm pay.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the ground is tilting under him.
S1.quote: My zone captain role is mostly answering new couriers' questions, and a chatbot could do that tomorrow.
fieldNote: He spots the **thinking parts** of his job, like onboarding, going first.
The **bus licence** is a real scheme he has seen a friend use.
He leans on Sofia's **steadier care job** and feels guilty about it.

steps.text: Apply to the county's free bus driver licence scheme
Use a chatbot more for emails and council forms
Go to every union meeting about app pay rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, and fast, because two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd be marching, honestly. I'd say it at the depot and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AGI bit in 2028 kills the zone captain job and probably the app's support staff. But robots by 2031 is what ends me, because self-driving cars and those little pavement robots would take food delivery. And buses would be robots by then too, so my bus plan doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the bus licence, because three or four years of steady wages beats nothing. I'd cut takeaway nights if bus shifts came through, and save every bit I could. Sofia and I would put off moving to a bigger place, which we'd been talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not panic, but scared in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said buses would be robots too. Why still do the licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because 2031 isn't 2028, and three years of a proper wage is three years of saving. I'm not pretending the bus job is a career anymore. It's a bridge, and I'd need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we keep the flat and park the bigger place for now. She'd probably say her job's safe, so we'd manage. I'd want to believe her.

say: We need something like a **basic income**, because two years isn't enough.
I'd be **marching**, at work and online.
think: AGI in 2028 ends the captain bonus; **robots in 2031** end the driving.
Buses go robot too, so the **bus plan** is only a bridge.
do: Do the **bus licence** anyway for a few years of steady wages.
**Save** every spare pound once bus shifts start.
Shelve the move to a **bigger flat** with Sofia.
feel: **Scared** in his chest, though not panicking.
S2.quote: I'm not pretending the bus job is a career anymore. It's a bridge, and I'd need one.
fieldNote: He spots the flaw in his own plan himself: **buses** go robot too.
He still takes it, valuing **three years** of steady pay as a bridge.
Sofia's job is the household's **anchor** in his mind.

steps.text: Take the county bus licence for a few years of steady pay
Save the extra from bus shifts in a separate account
Put off moving to a bigger flat with Sofia
Join marches calling for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up proper retraining, if the government starts now. I'd push the union to ask for that. Not just talk, money on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus the three for robots gets me to about 2034. That's long enough to try something real, not just a bridge. I've always liked fixing my car, so maybe I'd look at electrics, like installing chargers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the bus licence this year for steadier money, then do a night course in electrics. Sofia and I would keep our spending where it is and put the bus money toward the course. By the time robots come, I'd want a trade where you're in somebody's house fixing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It feels like a plan, not just bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrics and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's always a fuse box that's wrong, and every house round here is old. My uncle did it for thirty years and never went short. Robots might get there one day, but not in old cottages with crooked walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, to study, probably. I already ask it to explain things when I'm stuck on a form. If it can explain wiring diagrams to me at midnight, that's useful.

say: Five years is enough for **proper retraining**, if government starts now.
The union should demand **real money**, not just talk.
think: Robots around **2034** gives time to try a real trade, not just a bridge.
Old **cottages** with crooked walls will be the last place robots reach.
do: Take the **bus licence** this year for steadier pay.
Start a **night course** in electrics paid from bus wages.
Use **AI** to help with study and wiring diagrams.
feel: **Uneasy but breathing**, because it now feels like a plan.
S3.quote: Robots might get there one day, but not in old cottages with crooked walls.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan from a **bridge** into a **trade**.
His uncle's career in **electrics** gives him a model to follow.
He sees AI as a **study aid**, matching his steady approach.

steps.text: Take the county bus licence this year
Start a night course in domestic electrics
Use a chatbot to explain wiring diagrams while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we plan, so there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind. I'd say it to the couriers' chat, especially the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years plus three for robots is 2039, and I'd be 40. That's honestly long enough that I'd probably have left driving anyway. It's not the robots that worry me, it's whether I'd ever have any savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my time: keep couriering a couple of years, then start the electrics course part-time. I'd also want to finally get a proper pension started, even a small one. And if Sofia and I are settled, we might think about kids around 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the work side. Still uneasy about money, because that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Does the timing change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one I'd put kids off for sure. In this one, there's time to get a trade first and then think about kids. I'd want a steady wage before a baby, whatever the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young couriers, the 19-year-olds who think apps are a career. They've got ten years, but they won't use it unless someone tells them. I'd tell them myself.

say: Ten years is plenty, so there's **no excuse** for leaving people behind.
I'd tell the **young couriers** to use the time.
think: By **2039** I'd be 40 and would likely have left driving anyway.
My real worry is still whether I'd have any **savings** by then, not robots.
do: Keep couriering **two years**, then start electrics part-time.
Start a **small pension**, however little goes in.
Plan for **children** around 30, after the trade.
S4.quote: In the fast one I'd put kids off for sure. In this one, there's time to get a trade first and then think about kids.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets him think about **family plans** again.
Money worry, not AI, is the **constant** across his answers.
He wants to **mentor** the youngest couriers, fitting his captain role.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrics course in two years
Open a small pension and pay in monthly
Plan to have children with Sofia after getting a trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even my backup plan, the buses, would be gone too. What would help is free training with a wage while you do it, and some kind of income floor so you're not choosing between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the waiting. Half my evening is sat outside a restaurant unpaid. Before anyone talks about robots, pay us for the time the app keeps us standing there.

headlineQuote: Half my evening is sat outside a restaurant unpaid. Before anyone talks about robots, pay us for the time the app keeps us standing there.
portrait: David is 27, does **parcels by day** and takeaway at night around Halford, and is an app zone captain.
He lives with **Sofia**, a care worker whose steadier wage keeps their flat afloat.
He is **steady**: uses AI now and then, and backs the courier union campaign.
His plans move from a **bus bridge** under fast AGI to an **electrics trade** with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 would take both delivery and his bus backup.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** with a wage, plus an **income floor** during retraining.
